passage.bullet: Volcanic highlands supplied black obsidian, green jade, and emerald quetzal feathers → prized across Mesoamerica
Hot rainforest lowlands and flat Yucatán limestone plains → offered timber, building stone, and farmland
Rivers and trails linked all three zones → villages swapped goods and grew into cities

context.bullet: Maya builders had no metal ploughs or wheeled carts → human skill powered every early settlement
Highland obsidian cut sharper than iron → lowland farmers traded crops to get volcanic blades

stems.stem: In the southern volcanic highlands, workers gathered ____________ and ____________ to trade with neighbouring regions.
North of the mountains lay the hot ____________ and the flat ____________ built on limestone rock.
Because trails and rivers linked all three zones, early villages could ____________ and grow into ____________.

lesson_1.watch_out: Maya lands were not all steaming jungle—they stretched across cool volcanic mountains, rainforest lowlands, and dry limestone plains.

passage.bullet: Natural cenote sinkholes, plastered Tikal reservoirs, and underground chultuns → stored water through dry months
Raised wetland beds and stepped hillside terraces → created fertile farmland across swamps and slopes
Maize poles, soil-enriching beans, and shady squash leaves → grew together to feed huge populations

context.bullet: Porous Yucatán limestone drained rainwater underground → cities collapsed without clever stone water storage
Farmers worked without oxen or iron ploughs → companion planting boosted harvests using wooden digging sticks

stems.stem: Since rainwater drained straight through porous rock, families relied on deep ____________ and plastered ____________.
Through Three Sisters farming, tall ____________ supported climbing ____________, while wide ____________ kept soil damp.
Combining clever water storage with ____________ and ____________ allowed Maya farmers to feed tens of thousands.

lesson_1.watch_out: Cenotes were natural limestone sinkholes formed underground—do not confuse them with human-made stone reservoirs and chultuns at Tikal.

passage.bullet: Uxmal and Tikal raised tall limestone step-pyramids and observatories → towered above busy market plazas
Anglo-Saxon families lived in small timber villages → kings ruled wooden halls, not stone palaces
Britons farmed with iron-tipped ploughs → Maya builders raised giant cities using stone tools alone

context.bullet: Ordinary Maya families lived in palm-thatched courtyard houses → only temples and palaces used stone roofs
Lowland and coastal traders filled city plazas → swapped cacao beans, cotton, salt, flint, and honey

stems.stem: Around AD 900, Maya masons at ____________ built tall ____________, whereas Anglo-Saxon kings ruled from ____________.
Away from the painted plazas, ordinary Maya families lived in ____________ homes arranged around ____________.
Even though Anglo-Saxon farmers owned ____________, Maya cities grew far larger with thriving markets selling ____________.

lesson_1.watch_out: Ordinary Maya families did not live inside stone pyramids—they slept in whitewashed, palm-thatched homes around family courtyards.

passage.bullet: Over forty independent city-states like Tikal and Calakmul → fought wars and formed shifting alliances
Each city obeyed a K'uhul Ajaw or holy lord → trusted to bring rain and harvests
Rulers performed ceremonies atop tall limestone step-pyramids → whole crowds watched from red stucco plazas

context.bullet: Like Ancient Greek city-states → Maya kingdoms shared gods and writing yet ruled themselves independently
City-states battled to control river trails → winning rulers taxed jade, obsidian, and cacao trade

stems.stem: Between AD 250 and 900, the Classic Maya lived in over forty ____________ such as ____________ and ____________.
Citizens obeyed a holy ruler titled ____________ because they believed he spoke with ____________ to bring ____________.
Standing high beneath narrow ____________ atop limestone pyramids, kings led ceremonies above ____________.

lesson_2.watch_out: Never call the Classic Maya a single united empire—each city-state had its own independent Ajaw king and rival army.

passage.bullet: Crowned aged twelve, Pakal ruled Palenque for sixty-eight years → built white palaces and a tower
Masons sealed Pakal's coffin beneath the Temple of the Inscriptions → honoured his sacred royal power
A life-sized green jade mosaic mask covered Pakal's face → displayed royal wealth and eternal life

context.bullet: Jade and quetzal feathers came from distant volcanic highlands → proved Palenque commanded long-distance trade
Most Maya pyramids hosted open-air rituals on top → Pakal's hidden pyramid tomb was unusually grand

stems.stem: After taking the throne aged twelve in AD 615, ____________ transformed Palenque by building ____________.
Beneath the ____________, archaeologists climbed down a secret stairway to discover Pakal's ____________.
Covering the dead king's face with a ____________ and ____________ showed how deeply citizens revered their ruler.

lesson_2.watch_out: Unlike Egyptian pyramids built purely as tombs, most Maya step-pyramids were topped by working temples—Pakal’s tomb inside one was special.

passage.bullet: Lady Sak K'uk' governed Palenque and crowned young Pakal → kept the royal dynasty stable
Lady Six Sky rebuilt Naranjo in AD 682 → carved stelae show her victorious like a king
Vivid Bonampak murals show horns, turtle-shell drums, and jaguar-pelt dancers → courts united nobles through feasts

context.bullet: Spotted jaguar pelts and woven lowland cotton → turned palace feasts into displays of royal status
Royal women moved between rival city-states like Dos Pilas and Naranjo → sealed powerful peace alliances

stems.stem: Powerful royal women shaped kingdoms, including ____________ at Palenque and ____________, who rebuilt ____________.
Tall limestone ____________ proved women could wield supreme authority by showing them holding ____________.
Painted walls at ____________ reveal noisy court celebrations featuring ____________, ____________, and nobles dressed in jaguar pelts.

lesson_2.watch_out: Do not assume only men held power in Maya cities—women like Lady Six Sky ruled, led wars, and appeared on royal stone stelae.

passage.bullet: Over 800 glyphs mixed whole-word signs with syllable sounds → scribes could spell any spoken sentence
Masons chiselled royal births and wars onto stelae and Copán's 63-step stairway → proclaimed kingly power
Turkey-quill brushes painted lime-coated fig-bark paper → created accordion-folded codices like the Dresden Codex

context.bullet: Maya scribes built ancient America's fullest writing system → preserved exact royal names and dates
Ajaw kings and queens funded trained scribes → stone monuments proved their right to rule

stems.stem: By combining signs for whole words with signs for ____________, skilled scribes mastered over ____________.
Across plazas like Copán, carvers chiselled royal histories onto ____________ and the ____________.
To make folded ____________, makers beat inner ____________, coated it with lime paste, and painted with ____________.

lesson_3.watch_out: Maya glyphs were not simple picture drawings—they combined word signs and syllable sounds to spell complete spoken Mayan sentences.

passage.bullet: A shell meant zero, a dot meant one, and a bar equalled five → wrote huge sums
Base-20 columns stacked ones, twenties, and four hundreds upward → place-value zero held empty rows
Fast bark-paper sums helped traders count cacao beans → let architects measure giant stone pyramids

context.bullet: Roman and Anglo-Saxon numerals had no zero at all → Maya place-value maths calculated far faster
Counting ten fingers and ten toes inspired base-20 → differed from modern base-10 tens and hundreds

stems.stem: Using just three signs, Maya mathematicians drew a ____________ for zero, a ____________ for one, and a ____________ for five.
Rather than using base-10, scribes stacked numbers upward in ____________ columns of ones, ____________, and four hundreds.
Inventing place-value zero centuries before Europe helped merchants ____________ and builders ____________.

lesson_3.watch_out: Maya numbers stacked vertically in powers of twenty rather than reading left-to-right in tens—one dot on the second row meant twenty, not ten!

passage.bullet: Narrow dome windows inside Chichén Itzá's El Caracol → tracked bright Venus without glass telescopes
The 260-day sacred Tzolk'in meshed with the 365-day solar Haab' → guided festivals and maize farming
Both interlocking calendars aligned again every 52 years → marked major religious celebrations across cities

context.bullet: Place-value zero and bark-paper codices → let priests record planet paths across hundreds of years
Accurate solar Haab' dates warned farmers when rains arrived → protected vital Three Sisters harvests

stems.stem: Without glass telescopes, priests climbed ____________ at Chichén Itzá to sight ____________ through narrow dome windows.
While the ____________ guided holy festivals, the ____________ tracked the solar year for maize farmers.
Turning together like interlocking gears, both calendars returned to the exact same starting date every ____________.

lesson_3.watch_out: Maya astronomers worked completely without glass telescopes—they tracked Venus and eclipses using naked-eye sightlines built into stone towers.

passage.bullet: Soaking dried maize in limewater made nixtamal → softened skins and unlocked vital healthy nutrients
Volcanic stone metates ground corn dough → families baked flat tortillas and steamed husk-wrapped tamales
Roasted cacao poured from tall vases → made frothy drinks spiced with chilli and honey

context.bullet: Heavy metate grinding stones came from volcanic highlands → linked everyday kitchens to regional trade
Terraced and wetland farms grew huge maize crops → supplied every household's daily tortillas and tamales

stems.stem: Every evening, cooks soaked dried maize in ____________ to soften tough skins and unlock ____________.
Kneeling at a volcanic stone ____________, workers crushed softened corn to bake ____________ or steam ____________.
Unlike modern sweet chocolate bars, royal Maya cacao was poured from ____________ and spiced with ____________.

lesson_4.watch_out: Maya chocolate was not a solid sweet milk bar—it was a bitter, frothy liquid spiced with chilli peppers and wild honey.

passage.bullet: Dried cacao beans worked as cash → market judges checked shells to stop clay counterfeits
Human porters wore forehead straps along stone causeways → hauled heavy packs without horses or carts
Dugout canoes paddled rivers and coasts → moved salt, cotton, obsidian blades, and green jade

context.bullet: Shell, dot, and bar maths → helped plaza merchants tally hundreds of cacao beans quickly
Coastal salt, lowland cacao, and highland jade → united Mesoamerica's three landscapes in city plazas

stems.stem: Inside shaded plaza markets, traders used dried ____________ instead of metal coins, guarded by sharp-eyed ____________.
Because Mesoamerica had no ____________ or wheeled carts, human porters carried loads using ____________.
Wooden ____________ glided along rivers and coasts to exchange lowland salt and cotton for highland ____________.

lesson_4.watch_out: Mesoamerica had zero horses, oxen, or wheeled carts before 1500—all heavy goods moved via human porters and dugout canoes.

passage.bullet: Players chased a solid four-kilogram rubber ball → wore thick leather-and-wood hip yokes to protect ribs
Hands and feet were strictly banned → athletes dived to strike the ball off padded hips
Sloping stone ballcourts stood right beside pyramids → matches honoured the sun and rain gods

context.bullet: Latex sap from lowland rubber trees → gave Mesoamerican athletes bouncing balls unknown in medieval Europe
Ajaw kings built grand ballcourts in rival plazas → games settled disputes and united crowds

stems.stem: Because the solid ____________ weighed up to four kilograms, athletes strapped thick ____________ around their waists.
Without ever touching the ball with ____________, players dived low to bounce it towards ____________.
Built directly beside tall step-pyramids, roaring Pok-ta-Pok matches were played to honour ____________.

lesson_4.watch_out: Pok-ta-Pok was not football or basketball—touching the heavy rubber ball with hands or feet broke the rules, so players used padded hips.

passage.bullet: Popol Vuh gods kneaded maize dough into grateful humans → made corn farming a sacred duty
The Hero Twins defeated Xibalba's underworld lords at Pok-ta-Pok → helped the Maize God rise again
Priests entered caves and cenotes → burned copal resin for rain god Chaac near Xibalba's doorway

context.bullet: Maize tortillas fed every Maya family daily → explains why gods formed people from corn dough
Porous Yucatán rock held no surface rivers → farmers depended on Chaac's rains to survive

stems.stem: According to the ____________, mud and wood failed, so the gods finally kneaded ____________ into humans.
When the ____________ defeated the lords of ____________ at Pok-ta-Pok, the Maize God rose like sprouting corn.
Seeing deep caves and ____________ as doorways to the underworld, priests burned ____________ to ask ____________ for rain.

lesson_5.watch_out: Cenotes were not just drinking-water wells—the Maya revered caves and sinkholes as sacred portals to Xibalba and rain god Chaac.

passage.bullet: Northern builders at Chichén Itzá raised El Castillo → honoured the feathered serpent god Kukulkan
Four staircases of ninety-one steps plus one top platform → equalled all 365 solar days
Priests watched stars from the summit → announced exact maize planting dates across the plaza

context.bullet: El Castillo's 365 steps matched the solar Haab' calendar → turned astronomy maths into solid limestone
Masons cut exact calendar staircases without metal tools → proved advanced Maya geometry and planning

stems.stem: At northern Chichén Itzá, royal architects designed the great step-pyramid of ____________ to honour ____________.
Multiplying ____________ steps across four staircases and adding the ____________ gives ____________ days.
Climbing to the high summit allowed priests to track ____________ and tell farmers when to ____________.

lesson_5.watch_out: Do not forget the single top temple platform—four staircases of 91 steps only reach 364 until you add that final step to make 365!

passage.bullet: Every spring and autumn equinox, afternoon sunlight hits nine terraces → casts seven sunlit triangles
Triangles join Kukulkan's carved stone head at the base → a glowing serpent appears to descend
Crowds offered unfading Maya Blue gifts → celebrated spring planting rains and autumn maize harvests

context.bullet: Heating indigo leaves with white clay created Maya Blue → resisted tropical rain for centuries
Years of careful solar tracking → let architects angle pyramid walls to catch exact equinox light

stems.stem: Twice a year on the ____________, afternoon sun hits nine terraces to cast ____________ down the staircase.
Meeting the carved stone jaws at the bottom, the shadow makes ____________ look as if it glides to Earth.
Crowds gathered with bright ____________ offerings to celebrate vital ____________ in spring and harvests in autumn.

lesson_5.watch_out: Kukulkan’s serpent shadow only appears twice a year on the spring and autumn equinoxes—not every sunny afternoon at Chichén Itzá.

passage.bullet: Lake-bed snail shells prove severe multi-year droughts → emptied Tikal's stone reservoirs and ruined crops
Cutting trees to burn pyramid lime plaster caused deforestation → fertile hillside soil washed away
Fierce city-state warfare blocked food trade → families abandoned southern plazas around AD 900

context.bullet: Southern cities like Tikal lacked deep northern cenotes → failed monsoons quickly drained plastered reservoirs
Ajaw kings promised rain from the gods → endless drought broke citizens' trust in royal rule

stems.stem: Tiny snail shells from lake beds prove that severe ____________ dried up southern ____________ around AD 900.
Burning huge amounts of timber to make lime plaster caused ____________, letting fertile ____________ wash away.
Combined with rival ____________ blocking trade routes, these three linked pressures forced families to leave ____________.

lesson_6.watch_out: Historians reject single-disaster myths—Tikal and Palenque emptied gradually over a century through drought, soil loss, and war combined.

passage.bullet: Families moved north to Chichén Itzá and Uxmal → deep Yucatán cenotes gave reliable water
Postclassic northern cities boomed from AD 950 to 1520 → proved Maya civilisation never disappeared
Cliffside Tulum welcomed giant coastal canoes → merchants traded salt, honey, cotton, and bright feathers

context.bullet: Sea-going Caribbean canoes carried far heavier loads than forest porters → boosted northern merchant wealth
Northern architects built Chichén Itzá's El Castillo during these centuries → Maya astronomy kept flourishing

stems.stem: When southern plazas fell quiet after AD 900, thousands migrated north to ____________ and ____________ near deep cenotes.
Across the ____________ era from AD 950 to 1520, northern stone cities thrived beside ____________.
Perched on Caribbean cliffs, walled ____________ welcomed giant sea canoes trading ____________, ____________, and cotton.

lesson_6.watch_out: The AD 900 decline only hit southern rainforest cities—northern Yucatán cities like Chichén Itzá and Tulum thrived for another six hundred years!

passage.bullet: Spanish forces burned books and spread disease → yet island Maya towns resisted conquest until 1697
Over seven million Maya live across Mexico and Central America → speak thirty-plus Mayan languages
Families farm maize and weave bright huipil blouses → modern Maya scholars also read ancient glyphs

context.bullet: Spanish friars burned thousands of bark-paper books → only four ancient codices like Dresden survived
Maize farming and weaving link families from 2000 BC to today → show unbroken living culture

stems.stem: Even after Spanish friars burned all but ____________ bark-paper codices, island Maya towns resisted conquest until ____________.
Today, over ____________ Maya people live across Mexico and Central America, speaking more than thirty ____________.
Modern families keep heritage alive by farming ____________, weaving bright ____________ blouses, and reading ancient ____________.

lesson_6.watch_out: Never say the Maya vanished or went extinct—over seven million Maya people keep Mayan languages, maize farming, and weaving alive today!
